Lesson 0002 • Circuit Strategies

Low-Side vs High-Side Switching

The ECU does not "slow down" an actuator — it switches it. Where the switching element sits in the circuit changes how the circuit behaves under a fault.

Low-Side Switching

  • The MOSFET sits between the load and ground.
  • Most common in automotive circuits (N-channel MOSFETs are cheap and low-loss).
  • The load is powered whenever the switch closes the path to ground.

High-Side Switching

  • The MOSFET sits between the supply and the load.
  • Used when the load must stay grounded for safety (e.g., some fuel systems).
  • Often needs a charge pump or driver because the gate must swing above the supply.
Why the position matters

A short to ground before a high-side switch bypasses the load entirely — current is limited only by wiring resistance, and the fuse blows. A short to ground after a low-side switch keeps the load in series, so the load limits current: the load runs continuously but the fuse survives.
